title: Worst-case total imbalance of merging adjacent piles (max sum of abs(L - R)): cubic interval DP vs endpoint DP
problem_statement: Given n >= 0 and n + 1 non-negative numbers s_0, ..., s_n (pile sizes in a row; integers or rationals in the implementations), merge the row into a single pile by n merges, each of which joins two adjacent piles of sizes L (left) and R (right) into one pile of size L + R at the cost |L - R|. Compute the largest possible total cost over all merge orders. Equivalently: the maximum, over all full binary trees whose leaves are s_0, ..., s_n in this order, of the sum over the internal nodes of |L - R|, where L and R are the total sizes of the node's left and right subtree. n = 0 gives 0. With S(x, y) = s_x + ... + s_y this is c(0, n) for c(i, i) = 0, c(i, j) = max_{i<k<=j} [|S(i, k-1) - S(k, j)| + c(i, k-1) + c(k, j)].

input.parameter: n = number of merges (the row has n + 1 piles).
input.size_measure: n + 1 non-negative numbers. Complexities count comparisons of two size-derived values (the comparison model of the entry); additions and subtractions are counted separately in the caveats.

algorithms.name: cubic interval DP (every split)
algorithms.idea: Fill c(i, j) for the rows of piles i..j in order of increasing length; every row tries every split k, i.e. every choice of the blocks i..k-1 and k..j joined by its last merge.
algorithms.pseudocode: prefix sums P; c[i][i] = 0; for L = 1..n, for i = 0..n-L: j = i + L; c[i][j] = max over i < k <= j of (|(P[k] - P[i]) - (P[j+1] - P[k])| + c[i][k-1] + c[k][j]); return c[0][n]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^3) on every input: n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate splits; exactly n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 comparisons, namely n(n+1)(n+2)/6 inside the merge costs |L - R| plus (n+1)n(n-1)/6 between candidate values (PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 5)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2): the (n + 1) x (n + 1) table c and n + 2 prefix sums (PROOFS.md, section 5)
algorithms.correctness: The merge trees of the row i..j whose last merge joins i..k-1 and k..j are exactly the pairs (merge tree of i..k-1, merge tree of k..j), and such a tree costs |S(i, k-1) - S(k, j)| plus the costs of the two subtrees; induction on j - i. Correct for any sizes. Count, read off the code: a row of length L tries L splits, with one comparison inside each merge cost (|L - R| is computed as L - R or R - L after one comparison) and L - 1 comparisons between candidates; sum_{L=1..n} (n - L + 1)(2L - 1) = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, of which (n+1)n(n-1)/6 are between candidates. Proof: PROOFS.md, sections 1 and 3.

algorithms.name: endpoint DP (two candidate splits per row)
algorithms.idea: For non-negative sizes every row has a maximising split at one of its two ends (Theorem 1 with Lemma 11), so the last merge of an optimal tree for the row i..j can be taken to join the single pile s_i or s_j to the rest: c(i, j) = max(|s_i - S(i+1, j)| + c(i+1, j), |S(i, j-1) - s_j| + c(i, j-1)).
algorithms.pseudocode: as the cubic DP, but for j - i >= 2 the maximum runs over k in {i+1, j} only; c[i][i+1] = |s_i - s_(i+1)|
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n^2) on every input: n^2 candidate splits; exactly n(3n-1)/2 comparisons, namely n^2 inside the merge costs plus n(n-1)/2 between candidate values (PROOFS.md, sections 2 and 5)
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(n^2): the (n + 1) x (n + 1) table c and n + 2 prefix sums (PROOFS.md, section 5)
algorithms.correctness: theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights: for split-dependent weights w(i, k, j) that satisfy the weak rotation condition RS3w (at every index tuple i < a < k < b <= j, if both rotation changes Delta_R and Delta_L are <= 0 then Delta_R = 0), every interval of the max-recurrence c(i, j) = max_{i<k<=j} [w(i, k, j) + c(i, k-1) + c(k, j)] has a maximiser k in {i+1, j} (Theorem 1; proof by rotations at the root of an optimal tree). Lemma 11 of the same note proves, for w(i, k, j) = |S(i, k-1) - S(k, j)| with all sizes >= 0, that Delta_R <= 0 and Delta_L <= 0 imply Delta_R = Delta_L = 0, so RS3w holds. This weight does not satisfy the stronger condition RS3 in general (sizes (1, 0, 1, 2): Delta_R = 2, Delta_L = -3), so Corollary 2 alone would not suffice. Restricting the maximum to the two end splits therefore does not change c(i, j), and some optimal merge tree is a caterpillar. Without the precondition the restriction can fail: sizes (0, -1, 1, 0) give the optimum 4 and the endpoint value 3. Count: one merge-cost comparison for each of the n rows of length 1, and two merge-cost comparisons plus one candidate comparison for each of the n(n-1)/2 rows of length >= 2. Proof: README, section 'Correctness of the endpoint DP', from Theorem 1 and Lemma 11 of the note; PROOFS.md, sections 2 and 4.

relationship: The cubic interval DP tries all splits of every row, Theta(n^3); for non-negative sizes the endpoint law (Theorem 1 with Lemma 11) leaves two candidate splits per row, which gives Theta(n^2). Exact comparison counts on every input: n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 vs n(3n-1)/2 (each merge cost |L - R| counted as one comparison); counting only the comparisons between candidate values, (n+1)n(n-1)/6 vs n(n-1)/2. Proofs: PROOFS.md and theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights.

sources.title: Maximum weight triangulation of a special convex polygon
sources.venue: 20th European Workshop on Computational Geometry (EWCG 2004), Seville
sources.note: Credit: Lemma 1 (in a semi-circled convex polygon, one of the two extreme edges belongs to a maximum weight triangulation), an endpoint law for Euclidean chord weights; the entry max-cost-bst-recursion-vs-cubic-dp-vs-endpoint-dp writes its exchange argument out for inclusion-monotone interval weights (Theorem E'). This entry's merge cost depends on the split. The content of Lemma 1 is background.

sources.title: Dynamic programming: interval DP (title translated)
sources.note: Credit for a merge special case (background): code for the maximum total cost of merging adjacent piles at the cost L + R that tries only the two end splits of every row, without a proof.

provenance.note: No statement of the endpoint law for this merge cost, or of the endpoint DP for this problem, was found in the literature checked (README, section 'Literature checked'). This is a statement about that search, not a claim of priority.

verification.method: V1: the validator runs n = 0..10, 12, 16, 25, 40, 70 with 12 instances per n from 12 families of non-negative sizes (bits, small values with many ties, all zero, constant, wide values up to 10^6, one heavy pile, geometric, ramps, sparse, valley, peak, exact rationals). check() is an oracle written separately from the implementations: for n <= 9 it enumerates every merge tree (Catalan(n) trees) and costs it from direct sums; for 10 <= n <= 150 it checks an exact certificate (an explicit caterpillar costed from direct sums as the lower bound, and a table U accepted only if U(a, b) >= |S(a, k-1) - S(k, b)| + U(a, k-1) + U(k, b) for every split, which bounds every merge tree by induction). On every V1 instance check() certified both outputs: it returned True (the validator itself rejects an output only when check() returns False, and requires the implementations to agree), and tests/test_entry_merge_imbalance.py asserts True on the whole V1 battery (the validator's seeds, 16 sizes x 12 trials). tests/test_entry_merge_imbalance.py: exhaustive equality of the two DPs with each other and with the tree enumeration on every size vector with n <= 4 and sizes 0..4, n = 5 and sizes 0..3, and n = 6 and sizes 0..2 (10 188 vectors; every interval is covered because every contiguous sub-row is itself in the set), the exact comparison and arithmetic counts for n = 0..40 (cubic) and 0..80 (endpoint), each for all 11 integer families, the candidate-only counts (one seeded family per n, n = 0..30), the RS3 failure on sizes (1, 0, 1, 2) with the endpoint DP still exact, the table sizes and the size of the numbers (PROOFS.md sections 5 and 6), the split dependence on sizes (1, 1, 0), and the counterexamples of the caveats. Theorem 1 and Lemma 11 are tested separately by theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights/verify.py. V2 (measure 'reported'): the exact number of comparisons of two size-derived values made by the unchanged implementations, counted by the harness's CountingInt number type; generate_scaling draws one of the 11 integer families, and the counts depend on n only. Cost expressions are the exact closed forms: cubic DP n(n+1)(2n+1)/6 (n = 16..128), endpoint DP n(3n-1)/2 (n = 32..512); rivals cubic n^2, n^2 log n, n^3/log n, n^3 log n, n^4; endpoint n, n log n, n^1.5, n^2/log n, n^2 log n, n^3. No counted comparison happens inside a CPython built-in. PROOFS.md proves every claim of the entry (exact counts, correctness, time and space, the size of the numbers, the oracle, the caveats) and names the checks and ranges of each proof.
proofs: PROOFS.md: every claim of the entry (exact counts: sections 1-2; correctness: 3-4; time and space: 5; size of the numbers: 6; the V1 oracle: 7; caveats: 8), with the checks and ranges of each proof.
Exactness of the endpoint DP: Theorem 1 and Lemma 11 in theorems/endpoint-law-split-dependent-weights/README.md (written proofs; not machine-checked).

caveats: The endpoint DP needs non-negative sizes; the cubic DP is correct for any sizes. With a negative size the endpoint law can fail: sizes (0, -1, 1, 0) (n = 3) have the optimum 4 (the last merge joins s_0 s_1 and s_2 s_3) and the endpoint value 3. The direction matters: the same merge cost under MIN (min sum of |L - R|) is not covered, and there the endpoint DP is wrong on sizes (0, 1, 1, 0) (optimum 2, endpoint value 3). What is counted: every comparison of two size-derived values, including the one inside each merge cost |L - R| (the comparison model); counting only the comparisons between candidate values gives (n+1)n(n-1)/6 and n(n-1)/2. Additions and subtractions (exact, checked by the tests): n + 1 for the prefix sums plus 5 per candidate split (two subtractions for the block sizes, one inside |L - R|, two additions), over n(n+1)(n+2)/6 candidate splits in the cubic DP and n^2 in the endpoint DP, i.e. (n + 1) + 5n(n+1)(n+2)/6 and (n + 1) + 5n^2; index arithmetic is not counted. Theta(n^2) is the cost of the endpoint DP, not a lower bound for the problem; no lower bound is claimed. Exact arithmetic is assumed (ties are decided by exact equality); for sizes >= 0 every number the DPs compute lies between 0 and n times the total size (PROOFS.md, section 6).
notes: The weight |S(i, k-1) - S(k, j)| depends on the split (sizes (1, 1, 0): the row 0..2 costs 0 at the split k = 1 and 2 at k = 2), and it does not satisfy the rotation condition RS3 of Corollary 2; the proof uses the weaker condition RS3w (Theorem 1). Relatives: max-merge-cost-larger-part-cubic-dp-vs-endpoint-dp (merge cost max(L, R), same counts, proof via RS3) and min-merge-cost-smaller-part-cubic-dp-vs-closed-form (merge cost min(L, R), minimised: a closed form).

background.statement: In a semi-circled convex polygon, one of the two extreme edges belongs to a maximum weight triangulation; the exchange argument of the proof uses only that nested chords are shorter.

For merging adjacent piles at the cost L + R (an interval weight, the stone-merging problem), a 2020 article on interval dynamic programming gives code for the maximum total cost that tries only the two end splits of every row, without a proof.
